Proof:
Let $s \in S$ be an arbitrary element. By definition of pointwise operations, evaluating the right-hand side at $s$ gives:
$\left( \frac{1}{2} (f + g + |f - g|) \right)(s) = \frac{1}{2} \left( f(s) + g(s) + |f(s) - g(s)| \right)$.

We proceed by analyzing two cases based on the relative values of $f(s)$ and $g(s)$.

Case 1: Suppose $f(s) \ge g(s)$.
Then, by definition of the absolute value, $|f(s) - g(s)| = f(s) - g(s)$.
Substituting this into our expression yields:
$\frac{1}{2} \left( f(s) + g(s) + f(s) - g(s) \right) = \frac{1}{2} (2f(s)) = f(s)$.
Since $f(s) \ge g(s)$, we also have $(f \vee g)(s) = \max\{f(s), g(s)\} = f(s)$.
Therefore, the equality holds in this case.

Case 2: Suppose $f(s) < g(s)$.
Then, by definition of the absolute value, $|f(s) - g(s)| = g(s) - f(s)$.
Substituting this into our expression yields:
$\frac{1}{2} \left( f(s) + g(s) + g(s) - f(s) \right) = \frac{1}{2} (2g(s)) = g(s)$.
Since $f(s) < g(s)$, we have $(f \vee g)(s) = \max\{f(s), g(s)\} = g(s)$.
Therefore, the equality holds in this case as well.

Since the cases are exhaustive and the equality holds for all $s \in S$, we conclude that $f \vee g = \frac{1}{2} (f + g + |f - g|)$.
$\blacksquare$
